concepts.name: The purpose and importance of accounting
concepts.description: Book-keeping versus accounting; why businesses keep records; the purposes of measuring profit or loss; the role of accounting information in monitoring progress and making decisions. Excludes the users of accounting information (acc.fundamentals.users).

concepts.name: Basic accounting terms
concepts.description: Business, transaction, book-keeping, accounting, capital, assets (non-current and current), liabilities (non-current and current), income, expenses, profit and loss, drawings: definitions with everyday Zimbabwean business examples. Excludes the accounting equation itself.

concepts.name: The accounting equation
concepts.description: Assets = capital (owner's equity) + liabilities; rearranging it to find a missing figure; showing the effect of transactions (capital introduced, credit purchases, payments, profit, drawings) on the equation and on a simple statement of financial position.

concepts.name: Types of business activity and organisation
concepts.description: Trading, manufacturing and service activities; sole traders (including vendors and small to medium enterprises), partnerships and limited companies compared (ownership, capital, liability, control, profit sharing); the advantages and disadvantages of operating as a sole trader. Partnership and company details are in acc.partnerships.formation and acc.companies.share-capital.

concepts.name: Users of accounting information
concepts.description: Interested parties and what each uses accounting information for: owners, managers, employees, banks and lenders, investors, suppliers, customers, government and tax authorities (ZIMRA), club members, the public and environmental bodies; households as users (ZIMSEC).

concepts.name: The accounting cycle
concepts.description: ZIMSEC: the stages from transaction to source document, subsidiary book (book of prime entry), ledger, trial balance and financial statements; illustrating and explaining each stage in order.

concepts.name: Manual and electronic (digital) methods of processing data
concepts.description: Processing accounting data manually and electronically (computerised accounting, spreadsheets, digital documents and ledgers); the benefits and limitations of each for the original entry of transactions and for keeping ledgers; no specific software packages.

concepts.name: Storing accounting data safely and sustainably
concepts.description: Cambridge 7.3: digital applications for all or part of the records; the need to store data safely and sustainably and the risks of not doing so; manual storage, data storage devices, cloud services and other digital services compared (advantages and disadvantages).

concepts.name: Source (business) documents
concepts.description: Invoices, debit notes, credit notes, receipts, cheques and cheque counterfoils, paying-in slips, vouchers, bank statements and statements of account: what each shows, who issues it, and which book of prime entry it is recorded in; documents produced manually or digitally.

concepts.name: Sales and purchases journals
concepts.description: Recording credit sales and credit purchases of goods from invoices (net of trade discount), totalling the journals and posting to the personal accounts and to the sales and purchases accounts. Cash sales and non-goods purchases are excluded.

concepts.name: Sales returns and purchases returns journals
concepts.description: Recording returns inwards and outwards from credit notes (and debit notes), posting to the personal accounts and the returns accounts; returns in the trading section of the income statement.

concepts.name: The two-column cash book
concepts.description: Cash and bank columns; the dual function of the cash book as a book of prime entry and a ledger account; recording receipts and payments by cash, cheque, debit and credit cards, online and bank transfers; contra entries; balancing; a bank overdraft as a credit balance.

concepts.name: Trade and cash discounts; the three-column cash book
concepts.description: Trade discount (not recorded in the ledger) and cash discount (discount allowed and discount received) calculated and treated correctly; the discount columns of the three-column cash book and posting their totals.

concepts.name: The petty cash book and the imprest system
concepts.description: The purpose of petty cash; the imprest system and restoring the float; the analysed petty cash book and posting its analysis columns; the benefits and limitations of keeping cash on the business premises.

concepts.name: The general journal (journal proper)
concepts.description: Uses of the general journal: opening entries, credit purchase and sale of non-current assets, writing off irrecoverable debts, transfers, drawings of goods and correction of errors; layout with narratives; posting and interpreting journal entries. Correction-of-error entries are taught in acc.verification.correcting-errors.

concepts.name: The double entry system
concepts.description: Every transaction has two equal and opposite entries; rules of debit and credit for assets, liabilities, capital, income and expenses; classifying transactions and accounts (personal, real and nominal); recording transactions in T accounts.

concepts.name: Posting, balancing and interpreting ledger accounts
concepts.description: Posting from the books of prime entry; balancing accounts (balance c/d and b/d); the three-column running balance format; interpreting what an entry or a balance means; folio columns (ZIMSEC only: Cambridge candidates need not use them).

concepts.name: Divisions of the ledger
concepts.description: The sales ledger (trade receivables ledger), purchases ledger (trade payables ledger) and nominal (general) ledger, and which accounts each holds; why the ledger is divided; ledgers kept digitally.

concepts.name: Closing entries and transfers to the financial statements
concepts.description: Transferring income and expense balances to the income statement (statement of profit or loss) at the year end by ledger transfers or journal entries; profit and drawings transferred to capital; balances carried down to the statement of financial position.

concepts.name: The trial balance
concepts.description: The purposes and limitations of a trial balance; extracting it from ledger balances or a list of balances; deciding whether each balance is a debit or a credit; amending a trial balance that contains errors.

concepts.name: Errors that do not affect the trial balance
concepts.description: The six types: omission, commission, principle, original entry, complete reversal and compensating errors; identifying and explaining each, with examples.

concepts.name: Correcting errors with journal entries
concepts.description: Writing journal entries (with narratives) to correct the six types of error and other posting errors, without a suspense account.

concepts.name: The suspense account
concepts.description: Opening a suspense account to balance a trial balance temporarily; correcting errors that affect trial balance agreement through the suspense account; preparing the suspense account and the journal entries that clear it.

concepts.name: The effect of errors on profit and the statement of financial position
concepts.description: Statements of corrected (revised) profit after errors are corrected; effects on gross profit and profit for the year; corrected statement of financial position items (extracts).

concepts.name: Bank statements and updating the cash book
concepts.description: The purpose of the bank statement (from the bank's point of view); items the cash book omits (bank charges, interest paid and received, credit transfers, direct debits, standing orders, dishonoured cheques) and errors in the cash book; preparing the updated cash book (bank columns).

concepts.name: Bank reconciliation statements
concepts.description: The definition, importance and preparation of a bank reconciliation statement: unpresented cheques, uncredited (outstanding) deposits and bank errors; starting from either balance; treatment of a bank overdraft; causes of differences; the impact of digital transactions on the process.

concepts.name: Control accounts: purpose and the sales ledger control account
concepts.description: The purposes and types of control accounts; the books of prime entry as sources of information; preparing a sales ledger (trade receivables) control account with credit sales, receipts, discounts allowed, returns, irrecoverable debts, dishonoured cheques, interest on overdue accounts, contras, refunds, and debit and credit opening and closing balances. Reconciling control accounts with ledger lists is excluded.

concepts.name: The purchases ledger control account
concepts.description: Preparing a purchases ledger (trade payables) control account with credit purchases, payments, discounts received, returns, contras, refunds, and debit and credit balances; the impact of digital recording on control accounts.

concepts.name: Capital and revenue expenditure and receipts
concepts.description: Definitions and the distinction between capital and revenue expenditure (and Cambridge: capital and revenue receipts) with examples; how each is accounted for in the income statement and statement of financial position.

concepts.name: Effects of incorrectly classifying expenditure
concepts.description: Identifying and calculating the effect of treating capital expenditure as revenue (and the reverse) on profit, on non-current asset values and on working capital items.

concepts.name: Depreciation: causes and methods
concepts.description: The meaning and causes of depreciation and the need to provide for it (matching); calculating depreciation by the straight-line, reducing-balance and revaluation methods; choosing a suitable method for different non-current assets.

concepts.name: Recording depreciation in the ledger
concepts.description: Journal entries and ledger accounts for depreciation: the non-current asset account at cost, the provision for depreciation (accumulated depreciation) account and the depreciation expense; showing cost, accumulated depreciation and net book value in the statement of financial position.

concepts.name: Disposal of non-current assets
concepts.description: Journal entries for the purchase and sale of non-current assets; the disposal account; calculating the profit or loss on disposal and showing it in the income statement.

concepts.name: Accrued and prepaid expenses
concepts.description: The matching (accruals) concept applied to expenses: calculating accruals and prepayments, adjusting expense figures in the income statement and showing other payables and other receivables in the statement of financial position; ledger accounts and journal entries with opening and closing accruals and prepayments.

concepts.name: Accrued and prepaid income
concepts.description: Income such as rent and commission receivable earned but not received, or received in advance: adjusting the income figure, the statement of financial position entries, and the ledger accounts and journal entries.

concepts.name: Irrecoverable debts and debts recovered
concepts.description: Writing off irrecoverable (bad) debts by journal and ledger entries; irrecoverable debts recovered; the effect on profit and on trade receivables.

concepts.name: Allowance (provision) for irrecoverable (doubtful) debts
concepts.description: Why an allowance is kept (prudence); creating, increasing and reducing the allowance; the allowance account, the income statement entry for the change and trade receivables net of the allowance in the statement of financial position. ZIMSEC calls it the provision for doubtful debts.

concepts.name: Provision for discounts allowable
concepts.description: ZIMSEC: creating and adjusting a provision for discounts allowable on trade receivables (calculated after the provision for doubtful debts), its ledger account and its effect on the income statement and statement of financial position.

concepts.name: Valuation of inventory
concepts.description: Cambridge 4.5: valuing inventory at the lower of cost and net realisable value; calculating the value of inventory; the effect of an incorrect inventory valuation on gross profit, profit for the year, equity and asset values.

concepts.name: The income statement (statement of profit or loss)
concepts.description: The trading section (revenue less returns, cost of sales with opening and closing inventory, purchases, returns and carriage inwards), gross profit, other income, expenses and profit for the year of a sole trader in trading or service businesses; vertical layout; the names used by each board.

concepts.name: The statement of financial position
concepts.description: Classifying and presenting non-current (tangible and intangible) assets, current assets, current liabilities, non-current liabilities and capital (opening capital, profit, drawings); working capital; drawings of cash, goods and other assets and private expenses paid by the business.

concepts.name: Sole trader financial statements with year-end adjustments
concepts.description: Preparing a full income statement and statement of financial position from a trial balance with year-end adjustments (depreciation, accruals and prepayments, irrecoverable debts and the allowance, drawings of goods, closing inventory); the effect of a change in one balance on other figures; interpreting the statements.

concepts.name: Departmental accounts
concepts.description: ZIMSEC: the purpose of departmental trading accounts; preparing them in columnar form; apportioning expenses between departments on a given basis; the combined profit and loss account (income statement) and statement of financial position.

concepts.name: Manufacturing costs
concepts.description: Direct and indirect costs; direct materials, direct labour and direct expenses; prime cost; factory overheads; adjusting for work in progress; calculating the factory (production) cost of goods completed.

concepts.name: Manufacturing accounts and the financial statements of a manufacturer
concepts.description: Preparing a manufacturing account, then the income statement (cost of sales using the production cost of finished goods) and the statement of financial position with three kinds of inventory (raw materials, work in progress, finished goods), with year-end adjustments.

concepts.name: Partnerships: formation and the partnership agreement
concepts.description: What a partnership is and why partnerships are formed; their advantages and disadvantages; the importance and usual contents of a partnership agreement (capital, profit-sharing ratio, interest on capital and drawings, salaries, interest on loans). Dissolution, admission and changes to the profit-sharing ratio are excluded.

concepts.name: The partnership appropriation account
concepts.description: Preparing the statement of profit or loss and the appropriation account: interest on partners' loans (an expense), interest on capital, partners' salaries, interest on drawings and the division of the remaining profit or loss in the profit-sharing ratio.

concepts.name: Partners' capital and current accounts
concepts.description: The uses of and differences between fixed capital accounts and current accounts; preparing them in ledger (columnar) form and in the statement of financial position, including debit current account balances.

concepts.name: Limited companies: share capital and loan capital
concepts.description: Limited liability and the advantages and disadvantages of operating as a limited company; equity; ordinary and preference shares; authorised, issued, called-up and paid-up share capital; debentures (loan capital); dividends; general reserve and retained earnings (retained profits); shareholders' funds.

concepts.name: Financial statements of limited companies
concepts.description: Preparing the statement of profit or loss, the statement of changes in equity (share capital, general reserve, retained earnings: profit, dividends paid, transfers) and the statement of financial position (equity and liabilities extracts) of a limited company, with sole trader adjustments.

concepts.name: Not-for-profit organisations and the receipts and payments account
concepts.description: Clubs and societies: key terms (surplus, deficit, accumulated fund, subscriptions, donations); sources of income; preparing a receipts and payments account and its limitations.

concepts.name: Subscriptions and revenue-generating activities
concepts.description: The subscriptions account with arrears and payments in advance at the start and end of the year; trading accounts (or statements) for revenue-generating activities such as a refreshment bar, shop or project; deducing missing figures from them.

concepts.name: Income and expenditure accounts and the club's statement of financial position
concepts.description: Preparing an income and expenditure account (surplus or deficit) and the statement of financial position; calculating the opening accumulated fund; applying sole trader adjustments to clubs.

concepts.name: Single entry, statements of affairs and profit from changes in capital
concepts.description: Why some businesses keep incomplete records instead of full double entry, and the advantages and disadvantages; preparing opening and closing statements of affairs; calculating profit or loss as closing capital less opening capital plus drawings less capital introduced.

concepts.name: Calculating missing figures
concepts.description: Using total trade receivables and trade payables accounts, cash and bank summaries and expense accounts to find credit sales, credit purchases, expenses, drawings, receivables and payables from incomplete information.

concepts.name: Financial statements from incomplete records
concepts.description: Preparing the income statement and statement of financial position of a sole trader from incomplete records, using mark-up, margin and inventory turnover to find missing figures such as sales, cost of sales and closing inventory. Cambridge restricts this to trading businesses.

concepts.name: Profitability ratios
concepts.description: Gross profit margin, mark-up, profit margin (net profit percentage) and (Cambridge) return on capital employed: formulas, calculating them from financial statements, and what each shows. Cambridge accepts only the formulas printed in its syllabus.

concepts.name: Liquidity ratios
concepts.description: The current (working capital) ratio and the acid test (quick or liquid) ratio: calculating them and presenting each as a ratio (for example 1.8 : 1), and what they show about the ability to pay short-term debts.

concepts.name: Efficiency ratios
concepts.description: Rate of inventory turnover (times) using average inventory; and (Cambridge) inventory turnover in days, trade receivables turnover in days and trade payables turnover in days: calculating and explaining them.

concepts.name: Mark-up and margin: converting and finding missing figures
concepts.description: The relationship between mark-up (on cost) and margin (on selling price), converting one to the other, and using either to find sales, cost of sales, gross profit or closing inventory.

concepts.name: Interpreting financial statements and ratios
concepts.description: Comparing results for different years; interpreting profitability, liquidity and efficiency ratios; suggesting ways to improve profitability, liquidity and working capital; how inventory valuation, sales volume and prices affect gross profit; how other income and expenses affect profit; why profit and cash differ.

concepts.name: Comparing two businesses
concepts.description: Cambridge 6.3: the factors that may make the ratios of two businesses differ and the problems of comparing businesses (different accounting policies, sizes, dates, types of business, one-year data).

concepts.name: Limitations of accounting statements
concepts.description: Cambridge 6.5: historic cost, the effect of chosen accounting policies, and non-financial factors (workforce skills, location, economic climate) that the statements do not show.

concepts.name: Accounting concepts: business entity, duality, money measurement, historic cost and going concern
concepts.description: What each concept means and how it is applied in the records and statements, with examples of breaches. ZIMSEC lists going concern, historical cost and double entry (duality); Cambridge lists all five.

concepts.name: Accounting concepts: matching, prudence, consistency, materiality and realisation
concepts.description: What each concept means and how it shapes year-end adjustments (accruals, depreciation, allowances, inventory valuation, revenue recognition). ZIMSEC lists matching (accrual), prudence and consistency; Cambridge lists all five.

concepts.name: Business and professional ethics in accounting
concepts.description: The need for an ethical framework; integrity, objectivity, professional competence and due care, confidentiality and professional behaviour (Cambridge), and professionalism, compliance and Unhu/Ubuntu/Vumunhu (ZIMSEC); applying ethics in day-to-day business transactions and its significance to stakeholders and society.
